title: Bitterness: The Hidden Leaven From Cain To Esau

sense.text:
“There is one body, and one Spirit, even as ye are called in one hope of your calling.” What is going on in one congregation is going on elsewhere. These classes are not rehearsed, yet the same talking points come out in the 9:00 a.m. class and through the week, because it is one body in Christ and one spirit. The Lord puts the spirit upon the leadership to bring out the class that addresses the issue prevalent at the time.

That issue now is bitterness. In the midst of Passover the Lord revealed it, not just in the islands but throughout our congregations. The Deacon was about to bring out the same thing in his own class the night before.

precepts.why:
“There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man.” So we are not alone. If leaders see a spirit in one place, they have to understand that the same spirit is elsewhere. Bitterness is a very common thing that many of us battle with.

“But God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape.” What is the way to escape? Put a class on. Call a brother. Speak to your brother, to get that spirit off of you. A lot of times the devil jumps up on us and in our own mind we create a whole other reality that does not exist in real life. Talk to the brother, and you find that all that mess you were thinking and rehearsing was not even the case.

At the end of the class the same verse comes back: because every temptation is common to man, we should be comfortable confessing our faults to a godly brother. He may say he was dealing with the same spirit.

sense.text:
Paul first wrote that “It is reported commonly that there is fornication among you”: sin was a common thing in Corinth. Then: “Know ye not that a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump?” That leaven is sin. A little bit of sin ruins the entire lump.

Bitterness is the hidden leaven that must be purged. We are in the midst of Passover, and if it is not purged, bitterness grows into a root that defiles the soul. Many brothers who left the body and came out with crazy videos started with a root of bitterness.

“Purge out therefore the old leaven, that ye may be a new lump.” At Passover you have to examine the spirit and purge out the old leaven, the old sin, the old man, so that we may be a new lump, a new creature in Christ, following in his steps.

“For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us.” Christ is our Passover, and he left the example we follow.

“Therefore let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, neither with the leaven of malice and wickedness.” That malice is the bitterness. A dumb thought jumps into your spirit, the seed gets planted, it gets nourished, and next thing you know you have malice and hatred toward your brother. And wickedness, because it leads to sin.

“But with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.” Meaning: I have the bitter spirit, so I have to go to my brother and talk to him in sincerity and truth. That is how we purge out the leaven.

precepts.why:
“Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example, that ye should follow his steps.” That goes back to Christ being our Passover, sacrificed for us. He suffered for us and left an example, so as believers in Christ we must follow the steps of Christ.

Christ came to bring peace. Bitterness does not do that. So to keep the feast as a new lump we have to apply the scriptures and walk the way he walked.

sense.text:
“Seven days shall ye eat unleavened bread”: we have to eat it every day of the feast. “Even the first day ye shall put away leaven out of your houses.” That is purging the old leaven. We had to do it physically, but it is spiritual today: the unleavened bread shows righteousness, and the leaven has to come out of our spirit.

“For whosoever eateth leavened bread from the first day until the seventh day, that soul shall be cut off from Israel.” How do we eat leaven today? A dumb thought jumps in your mind and you say, I don’t like that brother. You are spiritually consuming it. That is how you get cut off from your people. This is a serious thing.

precepts.why:
What is the house today? “Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?” You, me, we are the temple of God, and the spirit of God is to dwell in us because our temple was destroyed.

So when it says purge leaven from your house, brothers dump out the toaster and sweep under the floor mats and into the corners. There is not a grain of yeast in the house, but the brother has an evil eye toward another brother, or he is bitter toward his wife, or vice versa. As we sweep our houses with diligence, we must do the same with our spirit.

“If any man defile the temple of God, him shall God destroy.” A brother will rebuke another in the street for having tattoos, saying he is defiling his temple. We know tattoos are wrong, but if you have a whole yeast factory in your spirit you are out of order too, and you will be destroyed just like that brother if neither of you repents.

“For the wages of sin is death”: that is how a soul is cut off. Whoever eats leaven, whoever entertains sin and does not purge the leaven from his house, earns that wage.

“But the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord”: Christ, our Passover, who set the example. That is the gift, the promise made to Abraham, that we can get repentance for sins, because we are in a wicked place.

“There shall no leavened bread be seen with thee, neither shall there be leaven seen with thee in all thy quarters.” We do not want to be seen in the midst of sin, whether it is Passover or not.

Some brothers do not throw the bread out; they put it in the storage closet, and as soon as Passover is over they bring it back into the house. Meaning they set their bitterness aside for the season and pick right back up hating the brother when it ends. That is not the spirit. That is why the leadership says throw it out. Don’t hold on to the bitterness; let it go. We have to get rid of it totally.

Brothers tuck it in: they tuck away their hatred and bitterness and save it for later, tuck it in when the Bishop comes around and are evil again as soon as he leaves. The leadership sees through all that.

“Know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own?” When we hide hatred, bitterness and malice, we are throwing that back in Christ’s face. He is our Passover, our sacrifice; he bought us back, twice. So we do not own our bodies, to have any angle to defile our temple.

When a brother lends you something, you take extra care of it. Christ gave us our bodies and bought us back again; we have to keep it like it is brand new. “For ye are bought with a price”, with Christ’s blood: “therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God’s.” Our spirit and our body belong to God. Holding back malice, holding hatred for our brothers or for our wife, puts that on Christ. It is not of the Lord, and we have to let go of that spirit.

The unleavened bread is eaten to remind us of something. “Seven days shalt thou eat unleavened bread therewith, even the bread of affliction; for thou camest forth out of the land of Egypt in haste.” The Lord delivered us when we were eating unleavened bread, meaning when we were not in the midst of sin.

“That thou mayest remember the day when thou camest forth out of the land of Egypt all the days of thy life.” Just because a sister throws down with the sweet bread, it is not about the taste. That bread is a reminder that we were catching hell in Egypt and got delivered because we were unleavened, righteous. If we want to be delivered again, we have to move in the same spirit.

sense.text: “Take heed and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and of the Sadducees.” Christ warned us of their leaven. What was their leaven? They were hypocrites, and they were following after the manner of the wicked. Leaven is an influence that spreads; bitterness is on the inside and it corrupts the spirit.

precepts.why: “The scribes and the Pharisees sit in Moses’ seat: All therefore whatsoever they bid you observe, that observe and do; but do not ye after their works: for they say, and do not.” What the Pharisees had going was hypocrisy. They say and do not. Whatever they tell you to do from Moses’ seat, do it, but do not do after their works, because of whom their works were after.

“Take heed, beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, and of the leaven of Herod.” The leaven of Herod lets you know they were following the white man, Esau. They were not just hypocrites; they were following after the manner of the wicked. That is why Christ said beware.

Many of the Jews who saw what Jesus did “believed on him. But some of them went their ways to the Pharisees, and told them what things Jesus had done.” Wherever there is good, evil has to be there: there were the believers, and then there were the coons who went and told.

The chief priests and the Pharisees gathered a council: “If we let him thus alone, all men will believe on him: and the Romans shall come and take away both our place and nation.” That lets you know who their masters were and whom they were following after, and why the class is titled from Cain to Esau. We see these things today.

sense.text:
At Passover sisters are good at checking the box, reading the ingredients for the yeast and the bicarbonate. We are good at checking the physical thing, but what about the spirit? We do not see the leaven inside of us: the sin, the hatred, the bitterness, the evil, the envy.

“For if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged.” If you judged yourself, you would not have to be told about your bitterness, or the envy, hatred and malice inside of you.
“But when we are judged, we are chastened of the Lord.” Now the Lord has to bring that judgment and that chastening, because you refused to get yourself right.
“She conceived, and bare Cain.” Cain was born first, just like Esau. The Lord was already setting it up; keep a mental note of it.
“Abel was a keeper of sheep, but Cain was a tiller of the ground.” Cain was out there working the field. Who else was a man of the field? Already it lets you know what is going on.

“And in process of time”: over time Cain brought “of the fruit of the ground an offering unto the Lord.” He already knew right from wrong, because his father taught him animal sacrifice. But in process of time Cain got evil and did not do what the Lord commanded.

Abel brought “of the firstlings of his flock and of the fat thereof”, and the Lord had respect to him, because he did what was right. Unto Cain and his offering “he had not respect.” Cain not doing right, and seeing Abel doing right, builds envy. It is the same spirit that was in Esau toward Jacob; it was already there in the beginning.

“And Cain was very wroth, and his countenance fell.” His countenance fell because he got corrected. Correction is what really got this thing started. Cain’s offering was rejected, just as Esau was later rejected.

“Why art thou wroth? and why is thy countenance fallen?” Cain knew that if he did right he would be accepted: “If thou doest well, shalt thou not be accepted? and if thou doest not well, sin lieth at the door.”

“And unto thee shall be his desire, and thou shalt rule over him.” Cain’s desire would be unto Satan, and Satan would rule over Cain. It is the same as Thessalonians, the one that comes after the working of Satan. The same spirit.

“And Cain talked with Abel his brother.” This is the deception. He acted like his friend: come on, Abel, let’s talk, tell me how your sheep look so good. Over a period of time he talked with him, then lured him out: “when they were in the field, that Cain rose up against Abel his brother, and slew him.” He deceived him through his communication, made it seem all good, to get him in position to slay him.

That is the spirit, that is the bitterness, and it turns to hatred. In wrath you will slay a brother; in bitterness you might betray a brother. Cain was the first recorded hater in the scriptures.

precepts.why:
“Correction is grievous unto him that forsaketh the way.” Cain forsook the way over a process of time, and the correction became grievous. That grievous environment created a spirit that nourished the bitterness, and it grew so much that he murdered his brother. That is the spirit you are rolling in when you move with a bitter spirit.

“And he that hateth reproof shall die”, because the wages of sin is death.

Certain spirits run with bitterness: envy, pride, hatred, evil suspicions. It comes bundled together, like a cable TV package deal, a whole network.

“Only by pride cometh contention.” Cain was contending because pride was on him. He would not make it right with his brother; his brother was making him look bad, so he had to put him to death. That is pride. “But with the well advised is wisdom”: with the ones that do well. Wisdom says, let me get my spirit right; I can’t have an evil eye toward my brother.

“For where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work.” That is the account of Cain: envying and strife, then confusion, so that Cain did not know right from wrong, and then every evil work: he slew his brother.

Confusion is Satan’s playground. That is why his children throw all types of confusion in the media and heap up dust wherever they go, and why some nations say they want none of that media in their land: every evil work is behind that cloud of confusion.

“Let us not be desirous of vain glory”: Cain wanted to be the man. “Provoking one another”: agitating a brother to play him out of position, because you are envious of him, so that he does evil and justifies your position against him. “Envying one another.”

We see that in marriage too. A brother provokes his wife, she leaves the house and does something stupid, and he says, I told you the sister was evil. No, brother, you are evil as hell; you provoked your wife. We are not playing that garbage.

“For sin, taking occasion by the commandment, deceived me, and by it slew me.” Bitterness is sin, and sin is only acknowledged through the commandments of God. The law says thou shalt not hate thy brother in thy heart, and when you meditate on it you see you have the evil spirit toward the brother. The law brings it to the surface.

You were deceived; you did not know the bitterness was sin. The law gives clarity. Like fog lights it pierces through the cloud of confusion, which is why the law is called a light. Then you see yourself in the mirror of the Bible: I was evil as hell. Some people do not like the light and love to walk in darkness: blue ribbon Christians in purple and gold, ribbon of blue and fringes, night walkers. We do not want to be that.

This goes for all of us; none of us is above it. When a lesson comes out, examine your own spirit and ask what in it pertains to you. Every lesson the leadership brings out is for us. As soon as you think, I am not dealing with that, Satan already has you lined up on his team.

“Cease from anger, and forsake wrath.” That wrathful spirit is the spirit of Cain, the bitterness. In that wrath you might slay a brother, as Cain did.

“Not as Cain, who was of that wicked one, and slew his brother.” Cain came back as Esau, the wicked, the throne of iniquity. If you are rolling in the bitter spirit you are moving in the spirit of Cain and Esau today. It is the same spirit as the scribes and Pharisees, who followed the Romans and were bitter toward Christ and wanted him put to death.

“And wherefore slew he him? Because his own works were evil, and his brother’s righteous.” Cain was a hater, the first recorded hater in the scriptures.

“We know that we have passed from death unto life, because we love the brethren.” That is why Christ gave the new commandment. “He that loveth not his brother abideth in death”: that brother’s home is death, the Edomite kingdom. “Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer”: whoever is bitter toward his brother is in the spirit of Cain. “And ye know that no murderer hath eternal life abiding in him.”

Even the scribes and Pharisees took on the spirit of Cain, of Satan. Bitterness will jump on us, but we have to deal with it; when we are overcome by it, we take on the same attributes Cain had.

“When the ungodly curseth Satan, he curseth his own soul.” Brothers and sisters say the white man is the devil, they will be destroyed, they are going into captivity, all while moving in the same spirit. You curse your own soul, because you are moving in the same spirit. Brothers talk bold against the white man and find themselves in that spirit through hatred toward their brother.

We have to exercise ourselves to have a conscience void of offence. Deal with your brother and sister uprightly according to the laws of God, and do not let it fester in your spirit until you are overcome.

Hatred is always masked, as Cain’s was when he talked with Abel. “He that hateth dissembleth with his lips, and layeth up deceit within him”: the brother talking all sweet, as if everything is all good. “When he speaketh fair, believe him not: for there are seven abominations in his heart”, because he is moving in the spirit of Cain. Murder, envy, pride and covetousness are among them.

“Whose hatred is covered by deceit”: that is why it is called the root of bitterness. Roots are covered by soil; you cannot see them. But “his wickedness shall be shewed before the whole congregation.” It starts where nobody can see, but the Lord always brings it to the surface.

“Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein”: try to set your brother up, lay a trap for a brother, sister or wife, and you will fall in it. “A lying tongue hateth those that are afflicted by it; and a flattering mouth worketh ruin.” The bitter spirit needs a lying tongue to mask its true feelings; even its flatteries are hatred.

“Be not hasty in thy spirit to be angry: for anger resteth in the bosom of fools.” The bitter spirit resides in the bosom of foolish brothers and sisters.

Bitterness is a progression. It starts with a correction or an offence, as with Cain. Then pride comes in and you will not speak to the brother; when you do, you speak with deceit, masking envy, anger and hatred. In the end it leads to your destruction and the destruction of those around you.
“A little leaven leaveneth the whole lump.” This is the hidden leaven: just a little bit of bitterness defiles your entire soul. It can be one thing.

“Beware ye of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. For there is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed.” Roots are covered, but nothing covered will stay hidden; the bitterness will be revealed.

The night the leadership arrived in the islands there was a heavy spirit of bitterness on brothers there, and they dealt with it for several hours. You think you are going to get the island vibes, and it is all manner of bitterness.

Leaven looks flat and unassuming in the pan, but over time as it bakes and festers it grows. A brother baking the hate, until he gets burnt.

“But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed.” Lust is not just sexual: lust for money, for power, for other brothers’ things, and lust for hatred, for keeping that strife and envy. Lust is an intense longing, an eagerness, and some people are natural-born haters, eager to hate; it is their whole lifelong mission. When you are eager about something you want to tell somebody, and so the bitterness spreads through the congregation.

“Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin.” It has been festering and baking, and now the root is revealed. A tree near a house sends its roots into the sewage line and defiles the plumbing; roots grow under a freshly paved walkway until a solid concrete slab is buckled up, and the smooth way becomes a stumbling block that makes people fall. No matter how strong your foundation, the root of bitterness can uproot it.

“Take heed, brethren, lest there be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, in departing from the living God. But exhort one another daily, while it is called To day.” We have to exhort one another daily in sincerity while we have the opportunity, because our life is but a vapour. Be genuine and deal real with the brother.

“Who can understand his errors? cleanse thou me from secret faults.” When you have that lust, you are eager and cannot wait to spread it. “Keep back thy servant also from presumptuous sins”: a particular lust can make you a presumptuous sinner because it suits your fancy, like the brother that likes to murmur. Tame that spirit: fast and pray, study, and ask the Lord to get that demon off of you.

“Let them not have dominion over me”, because if you do not, it will have dominion over you as that spirit had dominion over Cain, and he slew his brother. “Then shall I be upright”: not upright like the white man, standing upright with his soul still crooked, whom Christ called hypocrites. “And I shall be innocent from the great transgression”: speaking against what Christ commanded us to do.

Bitterness is dangerous because it is hidden, it grows, and it spreads. It is more than being upset: a deep, lingering resentment that settles in the heart and shapes how a person thinks, speaks and reacts. It shows as holding on to past wrongs for years, replaying the hurt, harsh speech, not trusting a brother, and quiet anger, and as coldness and distance, separating from the brethren once correction comes: I got to fall back, I got to take a break. You don’t get no breaks; you want a break because you want to sin. It comes from unforgiveness and pride, and it blocks peace and growth, opens the door to anger, malice and division, and distorts perception, so that nothing good is perceived. That is what led to Cain killing Abel.

sense.text: Rebekah had twins in her womb. “And the first came out red, all over like an hairy garment; and they called his name Esau.” He was already born with the mark of Cain on him, and he was the firstborn, as Cain was the firstborn. Jacob was not described, because he was the son of God and looked like everybody else; they had to note what Esau looked like. When the Bishop brought out that Cain is Esau, that is the proper understanding.
“Esau was a cunning hunter, a man of the field”: working the field, like Cain in Genesis 4. Crystal clear. “And Jacob was a plain man, dwelling in tents.”
“Feed me, I pray thee, with that same red pottage.” He wanted the red meat, as they like their steaks bloody red on the grill today. “Therefore was his name called Edom.”

Jacob said straight up, “Sell me this day thy birthright.” There was no trickery. Esau said, “Behold, I am at the point to die: and what profit shall this birthright do to me?” A man of the field is a carnal-minded man. He said, the hell with the birthright, which is from above, which is spiritual; he wanted the carnal thing. Right off the jump this was an earthly man.

“Swear to me this day.” Jacob made him swear because the word of the white man is no good; he will make an agreement and turn right back on it, hence the hundreds of treaties broken with Gad. Jacob wanted it certified: signed, sealed and delivered.
“Thus Esau despised his birthright.” He threw it in the garbage for something to eat. Food was his lust at that time; today it is money and fame, and they throw it all away.

precepts.why: “She conceived, and bare Cain”, and “she again bare his brother Abel.” Cain was born first, then Abel. In the same way, Esau came out first and then Jacob. The firstborn in both is the one with the evil spirit, and Cain “was a tiller of the ground” as Esau was “a man of the field.”

sense.text: “He cried with a great and exceeding bitter cry.” Now all of a sudden he is worried about the blessing. Why do they want to stand in our place claiming to be the Jews, the people of the book? Same spirit. Where was that energy back with your father? He threw it away for something to eat. This is the worldly sorrow.

“Is not he rightly named Jacob? for he hath supplanted me these two times: he took away my birthright.” Lying and playing the victim. We read that he gave the birthright away; now he accuses his brother. That is how they do today: throw a rock and hide the hand, and when they get hit back, run to the UN as the victim.
“And Esau lifted up his voice, and wept.” Antisemitism: the same thing, the same spirit.

“Thy dwelling shall be the fatness of the earth”: they would live in the best places. “And by thy sword shalt thou live”: that is how they get the best places of the earth, by the sword, not by voting. He conquered, destroyed, decimated, and replaced. “And it shall come to pass when thou shalt have the dominion, that thou shalt break his yoke from off thy neck.”

“And Esau hated Jacob because of the blessing”: this is the bitterness. “And Esau said in his heart, The days of mourning for my father are at hand; then will I slay my brother Jacob.” In process of time, the same as his father Cain in Genesis 4. Cain slew Abel; Esau wanted to kill Jacob. Cain was the firstborn; Esau was the firstborn.

precepts.why: Somebody can carry bitterness, hatred and malice toward you and hide it completely. After Esau said in his heart he would slay his brother, see how he acted in front of him: “And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept.” He was playing the long game, pretending to be on your side while waiting to hit you at your worst. They call that a liberal today: oh, we love you niggers, I mean black people. And Jacob gave him gifts because he knew Esau hated him and might be coming to kill him.

Was Esau tricked, as he claimed? Esau came “from the field, and he was faint”, and Jacob said plainly, “Sell me this day thy birthright.” Where is the trickery? It was up to Esau to say no. Esau said, “what profit shall this birthright do to me?” and sold it under oath. “Thus Esau despised his birthright.” So the claim that Jacob supplanted him was a lie.

“Thou givest thy mouth to evil, and thy tongue frameth deceit.” This is the so-called white man, the spirit of Cain, Esau. “Thou sittest and speakest against thy brother; thou slanderest thine own mother’s son.” That is the slander we just read: he tricked me two times. Nowhere does scripture show Jacob dealing with him in deceit. They were liars from the beginning, moving in the spirit of their father Cain, who was of the wicked one, and we must make sure we are not moving in that same spirit.

Esau had the worldly sorrow; he realized he wanted the blessing back. “For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of”: to our inheritance, and not to go back on it. “But the sorrow of the world worketh death”: the sorrow of the man of the field, the Edomite. We have to be sincere when we come to the Lord with godly sorrow, not faking the funk.

Here is the worldly sorrow. When the Lord increases the affliction, the one who has been wicked the whole time calls on the Lord: “Then shall they call upon me, but I will not answer; they shall seek me early, but they shall not find me.” The number you have dialed is no longer available. There will be no connection to the Lord on that day.

“For that they hated knowledge, and did not choose the fear of the Lord”: they had the carnal mind of Cain and Esau and cast the word behind their back like their father did. “They despised all my reproof. Therefore shall they eat of the fruit of their own way.” If you sow sin, that is what you reap, as Romans 6:23 said. Many of our brothers and sisters do this; we all have to examine ourselves.

They call Gad an Indian giver when he wants his land and resources back, yet Esau was the Indian giver: he sold his birthright, then wanted it back. And Gad never gave it; they took it through lies and deceit. It is the covetous mind of a child who sees another kid with a toy and cries that it was taken from him.

“He hath put forth his hands against such as be at peace with him: he hath broken his covenant.” Violence and war against people who are not bothering him; every treaty he signs he breaks, and he has been breaking it since his birth. “The words of his mouth were smoother than butter, but war was in his heart: his words were softer than oil, yet were they drawn swords.” We saw it with Jacob, in the Greek captivity, with Gad, and today in the land over there, killing peace negotiators.

Isn’t that the same as the bitter spirit? A brother offers peace, brother, I think you got something against me, and you say, nah, we good, while you fire a Hellfire missile, a drone strike, on any chance of peace negotiation with him, then turn around and call the white man wicked. Thou art the man.

Proverbs 1 said they would call and he would not hear; the parable of the ten virgins shows the same. The foolish “took no oil with them”: the oil is wisdom. At midnight, “Behold, the bridegroom cometh”: Christ has returned. The foolish said, “Give us of your oil; for our lamps are gone out”, and the wise answered, “Not so; lest there be not enough for us and you.” You are on your own.

“And they that were ready went in with him to the marriage: and the door was shut.” When the others came saying “Lord, Lord, open to us”, he answered, “I know you not.” You are not on the guest list. “Watch therefore.” We do not want that door shutting on us, as it did on Esau; we have to stay in the spirit. The theme is that Esau hated his brother, and we cannot have the mind of Esau.

Cain was the first documented hater, and Esau hated Jacob. “Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thine heart: thou shalt in any wise rebuke thy neighbour, and not suffer sin upon him.” If I love a brother or a sister, I have to correct them, because the wages of sin is death. Loving the brethren is how we know we passed from death unto life.

“Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people.” We cannot move in the spirit of Cain or Esau. Cain hated Abel; Esau hates Jacob, the so-called blacks, Hispanics and Native Americans. We are oppressed by the same nations, so what sense does it make to hate the man next to me? It is like blocking your own teammate’s shot. “But thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the Lord.” Those that fear the Lord will not do that.

The bitter brothers bear grudges, the very thing this law forbids.

“Whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause”, whosoever is bitter with his brother, “shall be in danger of the judgment”, the same judgment as the one who kills. Esau wanted to kill Jacob, Cain actually did it, and if you have hatred toward your brother in your heart, that makes you a murderer. So Esau was guilty of murder by what Christ said here.

“If thou bring thy gift to the altar, and there rememberest that thy brother hath ought against thee; Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother.” Before you go to the Lord seeking pardon, make up with your brother. Otherwise the Lord will reject your gift as he rejected Cain’s offering. Hatred for your brother is the fruits and vegetables Cain offered up.

“Forgive thy neighbour the hurt that he hath done unto thee, so shall thy sins also be forgiven when thou prayest.” Forgive first; then your prayers will be heard. “One man beareth hatred against another, and doth he seek pardon from the Lord?” Hatred for your brother, your wife, your leadership, while asking the Lord for forgiveness: it is not going to work. “He sheweth no mercy to a man, which is like himself”, one who falls and sins like you, “and doth he ask forgiveness of his own sins?” If you cannot forgive your brother or sister, Christ is not going to forgive you.

“If he that is but flesh nourish hatred, who will intreat for pardon of his sins?” “Remember thy end, and let enmity cease”: in the end we are judged by what is in this Bible and what we did on this earth. “bear no malice to thy neighbour”, and “wink at ignorance.” Brush it off your shoulders and let it go, the same way brothers have forgiven you and Christ forgave us of many idolatrous things.

“Abstain from strife, and thou shalt diminish thy sins: for a furious man will kindle strife.” A man who cannot forgive is a sinful man: he “disquieteth friends, and maketh debate among them that be at peace.” When that brother comes around, everyone’s defenses go up: here comes some bull. Only bitter brothers come with strife; brothers of peace come with the fruit of the spirit.

With a bitter person comes pride. “Bear not hatred to thy neighbour for every wrong.” To a bitter person everything is negative. The brother brings solutions and advice, but they want to see the brother or sister hurt, slumped down, corrected. “And do nothing at all by injurious practices”: harmful, abusive practices, like Cain’s murder of Abel and what Esau sought against Jacob.

“Pride is hateful before God and man: and by both doth one commit iniquity.” Committing iniquity puts you out from the kingdom of God. Esau is not getting the kingdom.

Operating in the bitter spirit you are blinded and keep on committing sin. “But he that sinneth against me wrongeth his own soul: all they that hate me love death.” We know Esau hates the Lord. Loving death is the love of the white man.

Cain is the first documented hater, and Esau came later and hated Jacob so much he sought to slay him. “For we ourselves also were sometimes foolish, disobedient, deceived, serving divers lusts and pleasures”: bitterness is a lust. “Living in malice and envy, hateful, and hating one another.” With the root of bitterness you are literally living in malice and hatred. Don’t be a hater. We learned that here in Babylon, this place called Egypt.

“For ye know how we have dwelt in the land of Egypt”: the land of our captivity, the gross darkness. “And ye have seen their abominations, and their idols”: the Christianity, the politics, the religion, the influences. Babylon makes you your own idol: my birthday, yolo, I got to do me.

“Lest there should be among you a root that beareth gall and wormwood.” That is the bitterness. Their idols defiled your mind with the carnal mindset; you picked up the mindset of the Edomite, hypnotized by his witchcraft here in Babylon, and now you have an evil eye toward your brother.

Simon wanted after the carnal mind. When he saw the Holy Ghost given by laying on of hands, “he offered them money, Saying, Give me also this power.” Like someone coming into the truth wanting to be captain, deacon or bishop. “Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money.” Money and connections do not make you an officer or put you above correction; the Lord raises up the men. “Thy heart is not right in the sight of God.”

“For I perceive that thou art in the gall of bitterness, and in the bond of iniquity.” Peter saw the bitterness in the spirit. Simon did not want the gift to heal people; it was the bitter, envious spirit of emulation: I can do it better, that brother up there teaching does not know as many precepts as me. In the bond of iniquity means in league with the white man, the throne of iniquity.

Bitterness becomes a hidden root that uproots relationships, the congregation and your marriage. When the roots go deep, it takes heavy equipment and chainsaws to get the stump out.
“Cain rose up against Abel his brother, and slew him.” Esau had hatred for his brother and thought to kill Jacob; Cain actually did it. The same characteristics that were on Cain are on Esau.

sense.text:
“Looking diligently”: not looking out over the horizon but looking within yourself. “Lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you”: that is the subterranean sin no one can see. Over time it springs up and troubles you; it distorts your thoughts and alters your perception of reality. Eyes once anointed with eye salve, to which all things were pure, no longer see clearly.

“And thereby many be defiled.” Roots grow underground undetected, then have a sudden manifestation, and the bitterness spreads and defiles others. Bitterness does not stay small; it grows underground and eventually shows up in visible ways, and it defiles not only the person but those around them.

“Or profane person, as Esau”: profane is relating or devoted to that which is not sacred, secular rather than religious. This man’s religion is sin. He is carnal minded, a man of the field. When the Pharisees followed him they were devoted to that which was not sacred. That is why he is called the son of perdition, the man of sin: everything he does goes contrary.

“Who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright.” When we roll after the carnal spirit of Esau we throw away our birthright, and the kingdom of heaven is our birthright. Following after the ways of the white man throws it away.

“He was rejected”, just like his father Cain, whose offering the Lord did not respect. If you roll in the spirit of bitterness you ain’t nothing but a damn spiritual Edomite. They always talk about being a spiritual Israelite; no, brother, with the bitter spirit you are a spiritual Edomite on the inside, always playing the victim.

“For he found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears.” Hold on to the bitter spirit and you will find that same place of no repentance. In the hour of temptation, when Christ comes back, people will cry for forgiveness, and it will be too late. The judgment is set.

precepts.why:
The parallel being drawn is the spirit that jumps on you when you move in this fashion. “He that committeth sin is of the devil; for the devil sinneth from the beginning”: that is the history being shown, from Cain onward. “For this purpose the Son of God was manifested, that he might destroy the works of the devil.” So why move in the spirit of the devil and think it is the spirit of Christ?

“In this the children of God are manifest, and the children of the devil: whosoever doeth not righteousness is not of God, neither he that loveth not his brother.” Scripture tells us how to deal uprightly with a brother when an offence happens, Matthew 18:15, not to sow discord and murmur and spread that spirit through the congregation. If you do not love your brother you are not considered a child of God; you are the son or daughter of Cain, of Esau.

The man of the field, the profane man: what is that called? “For to be carnally minded is death”: Edomite minded, the profane mind. That is why he is called the son of perdition. “But to be spiritually minded is life and peace.” Spiritually minded, you want to gain your brother. That does not mean always being buddy-buddy, but the scripture says instead of a friend become not an enemy. Brothers hold on to a rivalry and turn a brother into an enemy so they can get back at him. That is the carnal mind.

“Because the carnal mind is enmity against God: for it is not subject to the law of God.” The Edomite mind, the mind of Cain, goes against God.

There are the children of God and the children of the devil, the godly mind or the Edomite mind; no in-between. “But unto the wicked God saith, What hast thou to do to declare my statutes, or that thou shouldest take my covenant in thy mouth?” Why talk about In God We Trust and swear on the Bible while doing nothing according to the scriptures, with transgenders out there, putting two men together? “Seeing thou hatest instruction, and castest my words behind thee.” The carnal mind is at war with God, the battle of the spirit and the flesh, and that battle is within us too.

We like to go for the low-hanging fruit, a brother watching porn or looking at women, and not talk about bitterness, because that cuts deep. “For many walk, of whom I have told you often, and now tell you even weeping, that they are the enemies of the cross of Christ”: men with the mind of Cain and Esau, carnal, earthly, men of the field.

“Whose end is destruction, whose God is their belly.” That is Esau saying, feed me that red pottage, to hell with the inheritance. Like Cypher: put me back in the matrix, I don’t want to be liberated. “Who mind earthly things”: the man of the field, after the lust of the flesh.

“For our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ.” The children of God talk scripture and look for Christ, and our conversation must be tailored to that.

Cain was rejected as Esau was: “But unto Cain and to his offering he had not respect. And Cain was very wroth, and his countenance fell.” The Lord gave it the Mutombo finger. “Why art thou wroth? and why is thy countenance fallen?” Esau makes the same move.

“Hast thou but one blessing, my father? bless me, even me also, O my father. And Esau lifted up his voice, and wept.” The same spirit as Cain whose countenance fell when he was rejected: rejected, and weeping.

Many are defiled because bitterness spreads. “All flesh consorteth according to kind, and a man will cleave to his like.” That is why you see a group of bitter brothers clinging together like cancer in the back of the room. “What fellowship hath the wolf with the lamb? so the sinner with the godly.” The bitter separate themselves; it is all evil meant to destroy.

Signs of a bitter brother: first, he is easily offended and looks for offence in anything that is said. “That make a man an offender for a word.” That brother said this, I’m offended. Brother, you are not in the right spirit. And he holds grudges, which Leviticus 19 forbids.

The bitter are always revisiting past wrongs, digging up old ish like a plumber. “An ungodly man diggeth up evil: and in his lips there is as a burning fire.” That is deceit and constant hating: the banana lip brother, like Cain eating his banana in the field, I don’t like that. And they lack forgiveness, as Sirach 28 showed.

Another sign is quiet resentment, sitting back stewing in silence: the bitter bashful brother. “There is that destroyeth his own soul through bashfulness, and by accepting of persons overthroweth himself.” He says, yes sir, everything good, while the whole time he is thinking, I ain’t feel like doing ish for that MF.

When the root takes and grows: “Woe be unto them that are bound with their sins, and covered with their iniquities like as a field is covered over with bushes, and the path thereof covered with thorns, that no man may travel through!” When bitterness becomes that big overgrown field, nobody can reach you. It has overtaken your soul and you have essentially become a damn Edomite, with no place of repentance. Brothers bring scriptures and charity, coals of fire, and cannot get through. It is even dangerous to reach a hand in, because the bitter brother will cut you up, sell you out, put you to death.

“It is left undressed, and is cast into the fire to be consumed therewith.” As death and hell are cast into the lake of fire: the kingdom of Esau is where you will be.

Bitterness spreads like leaven, and one way it spreads is through words. Yeast makes things rise. “Be not deceived: evil communications corrupt good manners.” The root of bitterness corrupts your spirit and your attitude, and that angry influence spreads to others through words and attitude.

“Make no friendship with an angry man; and with a furious man thou shalt not go.” The bitter brother is like that dangerous brush; anything could be on the other side of it. “Lest thou learn his ways, and get a snare to thy soul.” He puts the bitter spirit on you, and now you have been bitten.

The offences of the bitter brother affect others. “But whoso shall offend one of these little ones which believe in me, it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea.” Brothers think offence means a brother out in the street, but the first offence is in your house, against your wife. “Woe unto the world because of offences! for it must needs be that offences come.”

“Husbands, love your wives, and be not bitter against them.” A brother can be bitter toward his wife. Then the whole family is destroyed: just as the root uprooted all that concrete, the house was a strong foundation until the root of bitterness came in. Now you inherit the wind. The leadership had to deal with this back in DC, and it destroyed a household.

sense.text: “And grieve not the holy Spirit of God, whereby ye are sealed unto the day of redemption.” Do not be the bitter brother who grieves the spirit. These are the signs of hidden bitterness.

“Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking”: bitterness comes first, and wrath accompanies it; evil speaking is talking foolish and reckless about the brother, the sister, your wife. “Be put away from you, with all malice”: put it away with extreme hatred.

How do we purge out the bitter leaven? The core scriptures were Exodus 12:15, putting the leaven out of the house, which is symbolic for your spirit, and 1 Corinthians 5, where Paul told Corinth the same. This brings it down to the practical level. If this spirit going on in the body is left unchecked, it can destroy the congregation.

“And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ’s sake hath forgiven you.” We read that in the law. You want pardon from the Lord while you have hatred toward your brother; Sirach 28 already answered that.

precepts.why: “Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering; Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye.” That is how we have to move: forgive one another.

“Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves.” Not peeping at your neighbour: examine yourself. “Know ye not your own selves, how that Jesus Christ is in you, except ye be reprobates?”

“The heart knoweth his own bitterness.” You cannot be confused when somebody asks where that bitterness is coming from. Don’t ask the Bishop to tell you what is going on with you. We can say, brother, you are off, there is sin in there, but you know exactly the specifics of what you are dealing with. “And a stranger doth not intermeddle with his joy.”

“Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts: And see if there be any wicked way in me.” Ask the Lord to reveal the iniquity in you and not let you be blind to your own folly. And how does he search you? The Lord is not going to come down and open the door to see what is behind it. You have to search the scriptures.

To get over the root of bitterness we have to confess it: I had the devil on me. “He that covereth his sins shall not prosper”: covering bitterness is like bringing in dump trucks to load more soil on top of the roots while they keep growing. “But whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy.” We all want mercy.

“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins.” This goes back to Leviticus: bringing your sacrifice before the priest was a public confession; you walked through the midst of all Israel with your offering. Now we have walls and technology and VPNs and think nobody knows, but the Lord sees right through it.

“Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much.” We should be comfortable confessing our faults, because no temptation has taken us but what is common to man. Confess, and a brother may say he was dealing with the same spirit, and you feel a lot better. Everybody deals with a level of bitterness, lust, lack of faith.

That does not mean a public announcement. Go to a godly man, a captain, a deacon, and say, I have this going on, I need help. He is not going to say, get away from me; that is Satan talking to us.

“For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you: But if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.” Offences are going to come; a brother or sister will say something and we will get offended. We have to have mercy on one another, because we are all sick. Two men in the same emergency room with the same sickness: one coughs on the other, and the other rebukes him while coughing himself. This is a hospital, family. If a brother coughs on you, forgive him.

How do we really put it away? “And be not conformed to this world”, because the white man rules over this world; do not have the mind of the Edomite, of Cain. “But be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind”, after Christ, “that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God.”
“Wherewithal shall a young man cleanse his way? by taking heed thereto according to thy word.” We cleanse our ways by taking heed according to the word.

“Wherefore laying aside all malice”: all malice, all leaven. “And all guile”: the fake talk, because you are bitter. “And hypocrisies, and envies, and all evil speakings.” We have to lay these things aside. “As newborn babes”, born again in Christ, “desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby.”

“Lay apart all filthiness and superfluity of naughtiness, and receive with meekness the engrafted word, which is able to save your souls. But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.” We hear the class about putting away all bitterness and do not do it.

Such a man is “like unto a man beholding his natural face in a glass”: he reads the scriptures and sees it, “and goeth his way, and straightway forgetteth what manner of man he was.” We do not want that. Look to the scriptures and say, Lord, thank you for revealing the evil in me, that I have a bitter spirit toward my wife, the leadership, my brother. Confess it, and pray to the Lord to remove that spirit.
